A covey is a small, tight-knit group — most commonly used for certain birds, especially quail and partridges, but also sometimes for people.
Covey as a group of birds

In its most precise, traditional sense, a covey is the collective noun for a small group of ground-dwelling game birds — most often quail or partridges — that live and travel together as a unit.

Think of it like a bird "family squad." A covey typically forms from a breeding pair and their young, who stick together as a close group, huddling, feeding, and moving across the ground as one. Over time, several of these family units may merge to form a single larger covey, but it always remains a small, tight cluster — usually somewhere between 8 and 25 birds.

The word applies most naturally to:

  • Quail (this is the most classic use — hunters and naturalists almost always speak of "a covey of quail")
  • Partridges
  • Grouse (less common, but accepted)

"The dog flushed a covey of quail from the tall grass, and the birds scattered in every direction."

"We watched a covey of partridges move slowly along the edge of the wheat field."

The reason covey is preferred over a general word like "flock" for these birds is specificity. "Flock" can describe any bird group, often in flight, often large. Covey signals: this is a small, cohesive, ground-level family group of these particular birds. It carries a sense of intimacy and compactness that "flock" does not.
Covey used for people (or other things)

Covey has been borrowed into general English to describe any small, close cluster of people or things. This is a figurative extension of the bird meaning, and it keeps the same spirit: smallness, closeness, a tight huddle.

"A covey of reporters gathered outside the courthouse, waiting for a statement."

"She was surrounded by a covey of admirers at the gallery opening."

"A covey of small shops lined the narrow alleyway."

When used this way, covey always implies:

  • The group is small (not a crowd, not a mob)
  • The group is bunched together (not spread out)
  • There's often a sense of the group being focused on something or moving as one unit

It's a somewhat literary, slightly old-fashioned word when used for people — you wouldn't hear it in casual everyday speech very often. But it appears regularly in books, journalism, and careful writing, precisely because it paints such a vivid, compact picture.
What makes covey different from similar words

WordWhat it suggests
  • Flock — a general group of birds, often in flight, often large. No sense of family or intimacy.
  • Brood — specifically the young of one parent; emphasizes offspring, not a social group.
  • Pack — used for mammals (wolves, dogs); implies hunting, hierarchy, strength.
  • Cluster — generic; works for people, grapes, stars, anything. No personality.
  • Covey — small, close, ground-level, intimate. For quail/partridges specifically; for people, it suggests a cozy or tight little gathering.

The distinctiveness of covey lies in that combination of smallness + closeness + specificity. It is never used for a massive group. If you use it for people, your reader pictures not a stadium crowd but a small knot of people huddled near something — maybe six reporters, maybe a dozen fans, not five hundred.

• A covey is a small, close-knit group — most precisely, a group of quail or partridges.
  • It signals the group is small, tight, and cohesive, not scattered or massive.
  • Used figuratively for people or things, it describes a little cluster bunched together, with a slightly literary, vivid flavor.
  • It is almost never used for large groups, and it is never used casually for random, spread-out collections.
